paper: Only three fingers write, but the whole brain works: EEG study of drawing vs typing for learning (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00706/full)
evidence: Electroencephalogram (EEG) was used in young adults to study brain electrical activity as they were typing or describing in words visually presented PictionaryTM words using a keyboard, or as they were drawing pictures of the same words on a tablet using a stylus. Analyses of temporal spectral evolution (time-dependent amplitude changes) were performed on EEG data recorded with a 256-channel sensor array. We found that when drawing, brain areas in the parietal and occipital regions showed event related desynchronization activity in the theta/alpha range.
claim: When children draw, their brains show theta/alpha activity in parietal and occipital regions, an EEG study found.
notes: Participants were young adults; claim generalises to children.
